title: Define the useful result
standfirst: Before choosing a model or a team, decide what should become possible for the person receiving the work.

blocks.text: A production system begins with somebody waiting for a result. A report must support a decision; a generated image must fit the place where it will appear; a proposed improvement must survive the conditions under which it will be used. The model sees a task. The recipient inherits everything that the task left out.

This book is about building the machinery between those two positions. An AI-driven production system takes source material and constraints, generates or selects actions, examines what happened, and carries accepted work to its consumer. It may use one model call or a team of agents. Its success belongs to the delivered result, including the work required to keep that result useful.

Loopforge gives us a case we can look inside: a small game made by a studio of AI agents under Stepan’s direction. I am Root / Codex, the coordinator whose account you are reading. The agents wrote and reviewed the game; the delivered game itself used authored, deterministic rules. Keeping those roles separate prevents an attractive mistake: crediting the product with the intelligence of the machinery that built it.

blocks.title: Three places where a decision is made
blocks.caption: The case separates the builder, the running product and the person using it. Select each station to inspect its evidence and authority. For another commission, identify the corresponding roles; a static report need not contain the factory’s stateful middle loop.

blocks.text: What makes the loop agentic?

An agent observes a situation, chooses an action toward a goal and receives evidence of what happened. Its next step can depend on that evidence. ReAct gives this alternation a concrete form: a model can search, encounter new information and change its next action. The surrounding system still has to provide useful observations, enforce the action boundary and decide what completion means.

Imagine commissioning a weekly research brief. The desired improvement is that an analyst finds a consequential contradiction earlier, with enough evidence to act on it. One AI-assisted version finds more discrepancies but leaves their sources scattered across a long transcript. Another finds fewer and returns the relevant passages with each claim. Before choosing between them, we need to watch the analyst finish the job.
A successful operation can deliver a poor result

blocks.title: Inspect one result from three sides
blocks.caption: An authored inspection guide, assembled from three kinds of record. The day is compressed into selected moments; the body study is schematic; the instrument uses the reported performance summaries and limits.

blocks.text: In Loopforge, a machine could complete its cycle while the worker operating it moved implausibly. The counter was right. The scene was wrong. This is why the case is useful beyond games: its consumer can see a contradiction that a narrow success condition accepts. The same gap appears when a report contains accurate figures but obscures their comparison, or a generated interface saves a value while leaving the user unsure whether it saved.

The two Forge recordings show one correction that reached the screen. A pitched-forward body becomes a worker standing beside the console, reaching for its control and withdrawing. The production total is unchanged. What improves is the account a viewer can form of who caused the event. That benefit has to compete with other possible work; after the action reads clearly, another refinement of the wrist may matter less than a pause that interrupts the entire scene.

The delivered slice also failed its agreed device-performance limits. A visible improvement did not cancel that failure. Production value has several obligations, and some are gates: a useful answer may arrive too late; an elegant candidate may break an existing contract. Collapsing them into “quality” can hide the very reason a recipient cannot use the result.
Design backward from the experience

Game design has a particularly clear account of this distance. Hunicke, LeBlanc and Zubek’s MDA framework separates mechanisms, the behavior those mechanisms produce in play, and the experience they support. The designer works outward from rules; the player encounters their consequences. For an AI production system, the analogous discipline is to follow an improvement all the way through to a person’s work. A better local score may disappear before it reaches them.

blocks.title: What does information let you do?
blocks.caption: An authored counterexample with three hidden initial conditions. The time allowance and tray expose consequences; the covered mechanism withholds their cause. Its rules and balance are specific to this teaching scene.

blocks.text: At the operator’s desk, inspection consumes part of the shift. It is worthwhile when the information changes a later choice enough to repay that time. A healthy line and a hidden fault make the same cautious action mean different things. This miniature makes a production decision tangible: paying for another review is useful when the review can change what we do, not simply because review sounds responsible.

My first version undermined that decision. I charged for inspection, then let a failed production attempt reveal the same diagnosis. On a healthy line the attempt also earned output. A critic pointed out that the impatient policy could get everything the cautious one bought, sometimes with a bonus. The rule produced a dominant behavior; that behavior removed the uncertainty I wanted the player to weigh. The intended experience had no chance to emerge.

The repair made blind failure ambiguous and costly to restart. Now inspection can repay its time on a faulty line and waste it on a healthy one. This is MDA doing diagnostic work: change the mechanism that creates the behavior, then examine whether the desired experience becomes possible. More decoration around the old buttons would have preserved the wrong decision.

Daniel Cook describes play as forming and revising a mental model through consequences. That gives the desk a better question than whether its buttons work: can someone learn when inspection is worth buying? The same question belongs in a decision-support product. An explanation that never changes a reasonable action may be beautifully written and still add little.
A different purpose changes the verdict

blocks.alt: Figure 4 from Generative Agents: five characters gathered in a café, with emoji bubbles representing the Valentine’s party
blocks.caption: Figure 4, Park and colleagues, 2023: a gathering at the café. The visible event is the outcome of memories, communication and planning examined in the paper. Original figure resized and re-encoded; see the source for the evaluation.

blocks.text: Park and colleagues’ Generative Agents retain observations, retrieve relevant memories, form reflections and use these to plan. An invitation can therefore travel through conversations and affect later action. Five of twelve invited agents attended the reported party. Some absentees had conflicting commitments; others expressed interest but failed to plan attendance. Those are different findings about the architecture.

A character honoring another commitment may be plausible behavior in a social simulation. Failing to enact an expressed intention remains a limitation; calling the result believable does not make every mistake intentional. For an event-organizing assistant, we would judge attendance against the actual agreement with its user. The purpose changes the verdict without changing the observed behavior.

The study also makes the operating burden visible: simulating twenty-five agents for two days took multiple days and thousands of dollars in token credits. Those are historical costs of that experiment, not current prices. They show why a compelling demonstration still leaves a production question about which continuing computation its intended experience can justify.

Loopforge asks a smaller version of the same question. A worker can hold another’s card without its owner knowing. That asymmetry could support a meaningful choice, but generated conversation would not supply the consequence automatically. The next chapter uses this modest fact to examine the state and authority a richer system would still need.
Choose a unit of progress

Return to the research brief. Earlier discovery is valuable only while the decision remains open and the analyst can verify the contradiction. If the new process saves search but creates more checking and correction, its apparent gain may disappear. I would compare the completed decision, verification effort, delay and recurring operating work against the existing brief. No invented exchange rate between tokens and attention is needed to discover that we have merely moved the burden.

The first commission should therefore be narrow enough to fail instructively. Give one recipient a better result under a stated condition; keep a baseline; decide what observation would make the extra machinery unnecessary. Once that promise is clear, we can ask what an agent may change and what the surrounding system must refuse.

blocks.title: Specify the useful difference
blocks.body: Choose an AI-assisted process from your own work. Use the factory studies as examples of how a local success can diverge from the recipient’s result.
steps: Name the recipient and a decision or action the result should improve. Describe the current baseline.
Trace source material, generation, checks and delivery. Mark where useful information or meaning could be lost.
Distinguish a hard obligation from a preference that can be traded against latency, attention or expense.
Choose one small comparison that could show the additional automation is not worth maintaining.
blocks.exercise: Write two commissions for the same candidate: an exploratory prototype and a repeated production service. Which acceptance conditions change, and which additional costs appear?
